l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: The front matter identifies The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII as Ovid’s work in a literal English translation by Henry T. Riley, with an introduction and notes. The introduction explains the purpose of Riley’s translation and commentary and discusses earlier English translations. The Synoptical View summarizes the principal transformations in Books I-VII, including the creation of the world, the Deluge, transformations involving gods and mortals, and the stories of Jason and Medea. It concludes with Jason’s recovery of the Golden Fleece, Medea’s magic and crimes, and the later stories of Ægeus, Theseus, Minos, and Cephalus.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: This work is presented as a compendium of the mythological narratives of ancient Greece and Rome. Its Books I-VII are summarized through their principal transformations, and the volume contains a literal translation with notes and explanations.

l: Ovid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Ovid is identified as the author of The Metamorphoses, which the introduction describes as the masterpiece of one of the greatest poets of ancient Rome.

l: Henry Thomas Riley, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Henry T. Riley produced the literal English translation of Books I-VII and supplied notes and explanations. He generally adopted the text of the Delphin edition while consulting the editions of Burmann and Gierig.

l: A Synoptical View of the Principal Transformations Mentioned in the Metamorphoses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: This section gives a book-by-book summary of the principal transformations in Books I-VII. It describes events from the division of Chaos through the stories of Jason, Medea, Ægeus, Theseus, and Minos.

l: Ovid’s Metamorphoses, Books I–VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: These books cover transformations and mythological narratives involving the creation of the world, the Ages of man, the Deluge, gods and heroes, and the adventures of Jason and Medea.

l: Greek and Roman mythology, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: The introduction describes the work as a compendium of Greek and Roman mythology and says that it conveys information about the learning, traditions, manners, and customs of antiquity.

l: God, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: The Deity divides Chaos into four Elements, assigns inhabitants to them, and creates man from earth and water.

l: Chaos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Chaos is divided by the Deity into four Elements at the beginning of Book I.

l: Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Jupiter slays the Giants, changes Lycaon into a wolf, and destroys the human race and animals by a Deluge. He later strikes Phaëton with a thunderbolt, assumes the form of Diana to approach Calisto, and carries Europa over the sea after assuming the form of a bull.

l: Deucalion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Deucalion survives the Deluge with Pyrrha. After the waters abate, he helps renew the human race by throwing stones behind him.

l: Pyrrha, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Pyrrha survives the Deluge with Deucalion and helps renew the human race by throwing stones behind her.

l: Deucalion's deluge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: The Deluge is sent by Jupiter to destroy the race of men and animals, except for Deucalion and Pyrrha.

l: Phœbus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Phœbus slays the serpent Python and institutes the Pythian games as a memorial. He is also involved in the stories of Daphne, the raven, Coronis, Æsculapius, and the transformation of Clytie.

l: Daphne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Daphne is changed into a laurel while fleeing from Phœbus.

l: Io, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Jupiter changes Io into a cow after ravishing her and entrusts her to the care of Argus. She later recovers human shape and becomes the mother of Epaphus.

l: Mercury, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Mercury slays Argus after relating the story of Syrinx, changes Battus into a touchstone for betrayal, and carries out Jupiter’s order concerning the herds of Agenor. He also approaches Herse and changes Aglauros into a rock through the consequences of his actions.

l: Juno, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Juno entrusts Io to Argus, places Argus’s eyes in the tail of the peacock after his death, and changes Calisto into a bear. She also causes Semele’s destruction, sends a Fury against Ino, and persecutes the house of Agenor.

l: Phaëton, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Phaëton obtains permission from Phœbus to guide the Sun’s chariot for one day. He sets the earth on fire, contributes to the darkening of the Æthiopians, and is struck by Jupiter’s thunderbolt.

l: Europa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Europa is carried over the sea to the isle of Crete after Jupiter assumes the form of a bull.

l: Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Cadmus seeks his sister Europa, slays a dragon in Boeotia, sows its teeth so that armed men are produced, and builds the walls of Thebes. After further calamities, he retires from Thebes and is transformed into a serpent with his wife.

l: Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Thebes is founded and its walls are built by Cadmus with the assistance of men produced from the dragon’s teeth. Its people later suffer through the fates of Actæon, Semele, Pentheus, and Niobe.

l: Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Bacchus survives the destruction of Semele, is brought up on earth, and is connected with the orgies and rites that Pentheus rejects. Through his agency, Alcithoë and her sisters are transformed into bats and their webs into vines.

l: Tiresias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Tiresias, who has been of both sexes, decides a dispute between Jupiter and Juno about the relative pleasures of the sexes. Juno deprives him of sight, while Jupiter gives him the gift of prophecy.

l: Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Narcissus rejects the advances of females, including Echo, and eventually pines away from love for himself. He is transformed into the flower that bears his name.

l: Venus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Venus intercedes after Ino leaps into the sea with Melicerta, allowing them to become sea Deities.

l: Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Perseus cuts off Medusa’s head, turns Atlas into a mountain, liberates Andromeda, changes sea-weed into coral, and marries Andromeda.

l: Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Medusa is beheaded by Perseus, and serpents are produced from her blood.

l: Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Andromeda is liberated by Perseus after he turns Atlas into a mountain. She marries Perseus after the sea-weed is changed into coral.

l: Arachne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Arachne competes with Pallas in the art of weaving and represents various transformations on her web. She is changed into a spider.

l: Niobe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Niobe prefers her own lot to that of Latona, after which Apollo and Diana slay all her children. Niobe is then changed into a rock.

l: Tereus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Tereus marries Progne, takes Philomela to his kingdom, and commits violence against her. He is eventually transformed into a hoopoe.

l: Progne, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Progne is the daughter of Pandion and the wife of Tereus. After Tereus’s crimes against Philomela, Progne becomes a swallow.

l: Philomela, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Philomela is taken by Tereus to his kingdom and suffers violence from him. She is eventually changed into a nightingale.

l: Jason, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Jason conquers the fire-breathing bulls, sows the serpent’s teeth from which armed men arise, and obtains the Golden Fleece with Medea’s aid. He later accompanies Medea to Greece.

l: Medea, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Medea assists Jason in recovering the Golden Fleece and accompanies him to Greece. She restores Æson to youth, tricks and kills Pelias after demonstrating her powers on a ram, later kills her children, marries Ægeus, and nearly poisons Theseus.

l: Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: The Golden Fleece is recovered by Jason with the aid of Medea after he conquers the fire-breathing bulls, produces armed men from serpent’s teeth, and lulls the dragon to sleep.

l: Ægeus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Ægeus marries Medea and nearly has Theseus poisoned when Theseus returns home. He later receives assistance from the Myrmidons sent by Æacus against Minos.

l: Theseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Theseus returns home to Ægeus and narrowly escapes being poisoned by Medea’s magic potions.

l: Minos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Minos interrupts Ægeus’s joy at Theseus’s return and wages war against him. He seeks the alliance of Æacus, who refuses it.

l: Jason’s recovery of the Golden Fleece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, front matter
s: Jason’s recovery of the Golden Fleece depends on Medea’s aid. He conquers the fire-breathing bulls, sows the serpent’s teeth, and lulls the dragon to sleep before obtaining it.

l: The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, INTRODUCTION.
s: The introduction describes Ovid’s education, career, friendships, marriages, and development as a poet. Although his father urged him to pursue law and public office, Ovid abandoned those paths and devoted himself to poetry. Around 8 A.D., Augustus banished Ovid to Tomi, probably because of the immoral tendency of one of his compositions and its connection to scandals involving Julia and the emperor’s granddaughter. Ovid died at Tomi in 18 A.D., and the unit concludes by listing his principal works, including the Metamorphoses.

l: Ovid, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, INTRODUCTION.
s: Ovid was born at Sulmo in 43 B.C. and was educated in Rome, later visiting Athens, Asia Minor, and Sicily. He briefly pursued law and public office at his father’s urging but ultimately devoted himself to poetry and associated with prominent poets. Around 8 A.D., Augustus banished him to Tomi, where he died in exile in 18 A.D.

l: Rome, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII, INTRODUCTION.
s: Rome was where Ovid was brought for education and where he spent much of his early career in the forum. He later left Rome under Augustus’s edict and never returned.
